title: Simple Pendulum
short_intro: A simple pendulum consists of a heavy point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible, and flexible string from a rigid support. For small angular displacements, it executes simple harmonic motion with a time period dependent only on its length and the local acceleration due to gravity.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Time period formula T = 2π√(l/g), dependence of time period on length and gravity, seconds pendulum, and simple numerical problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Effect of temperature changes on pendulum clocks, pendulums in accelerated frames (lifts, vehicles), finite amplitude corrections, physical (compound) pendulum, and center of oscillation.

prerequisites: Resolution of forces and torque in rotational dynamics
Taylor series approximation for sin(θ) for small angles

concept_notes.heading: Ideal vs. Practical Simple Pendulum
bullets: An ideal simple pendulum requires a concentrated point mass (bob) and a perfectly massless, flexible, and inextensible string.
In practice, every pendulum has a finite size (spherical bob), making it a physical or compound pendulum.
The effective length (L) is defined as the distance from the point of suspension to the center of mass of the bob.

concept_notes.heading: Equation of Motion and SHM Condition
bullets: Restoring torque about the point of suspension is provided by the tangential component of the weight: τ = -mg l sin(θ).
Using Newton's law for rotation, I(α) = τ, where I = ml² is the moment of inertia.
For small angular displacement (θ ≪ 1 radian), sin(θ) ≈ θ, reducing the equation to d²θ/dt² + (g/l)θ = 0, which represents simple harmonic motion.

concept_notes.heading: Seconds Pendulum
bullets: A seconds pendulum is defined as a simple pendulum whose time period is exactly 2 seconds (1 second for each-way swing).
The length of a seconds pendulum on the surface of the Earth is approximately 0.993 meters (or ~99.3 cm).
Its frequency is 0.5 Hz and angular frequency ω = π rad/s.

concept_notes.heading: Effect of Environmental Factors on Time Period
bullets: Temperature change: A rise in temperature increases the effective length of the pendulum (l' = l(1 + αΔT)), causing the clock to lose time and run slow.
Altitude and Depth: Since g decreases with height above the Earth's surface and depth below it, the time period of a pendulum increases in both cases.
Lift acceleration: In a lift accelerating upwards with acceleration 'a', the effective gravity becomes (g + a); in a downward acceleration, it is (g - a).

derivations.title: Time Period of a Simple Pendulum
derivations.conditions: Small amplitude approximation (θ ≤ 4°), rigid support, inextensible string.
steps: Consider a bob of mass m suspended by a string of length l displaced by an angle θ from the vertical.
The restoring torque acting about the point of suspension O is τ = -mg l sin(θ). Negative sign indicates torque acts to oppose the angular displacement.
Equating torque to rate of change of angular momentum: I(d²θ/dt²) = -mg l sin(θ). Substituting moment of inertia I = ml², we get ml²(d²θ/dt²) = -mg l sin(θ).
For small θ, replace sin(θ) with θ, yielding d²θ/dt² + (g/l)θ = 0.
Comparing with the standard SHM equation d²θ/dt² + ω²θ = 0, the angular frequency is ω = √(g/l).
The time period T is given by T = 2π/ω = 2π√(l/g).

derivations.title: Finite Amplitude Correction for Time Period
derivations.conditions: Large angular amplitude θ&sub0; where small angle approximation fails.
steps: Start from the exact equation of motion derived from energy conservation: (dθ/dt)² = (2g/l)(cos(θ) - cos(θ&sub0;)).
Expressing cosines in terms of half-angles and integrating over one complete period T yields the exact elliptic integral: T = 4√(l/g) ∫[0 to θ&sub0;] dθ / √(2(cos(θ) - cos(θ&sub0;))).
Using the trigonometric expansion sin(θ/2) = sin(θ&sub0;/2) sin(φ) and expanding via binomial theorem for small to moderate θ&sub0;.
Integrating the first-order correction term gives T = T&sub0; (1 + (1/16)θ&sub0;² + ...), where T&sub0; = 2π√(l/g).

graphs_and_experiments.title: T vs l Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve showing time period T plotted against length l.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms that T is proportional to the square root of length.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual identification of graph shapes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: T² vs l Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with a positive slope equal to 4π²/g.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The linear relationship allows precise experimental determination of acceleration due to gravity g from the slope.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical calculation of g from experimental slope data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Killed / Free Fall Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A pendulum inside a freely falling lift or satellite.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Effective gravity g_eff = 0, leading to an infinite time period (pendulum ceases to oscillate).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual testing of conditions where simple harmonic motion stops.

solved_numericals.question: Find the length of a simple pendulum whose time period is 2 seconds at a place where g = 9.8 m/s² (π² ≈ 9.8).
If the length of a simple pendulum is increased by 44%, find the percentage increase in its time period.
solution_steps: Let initial length be l_1 = l and final length be l_2 = 1.44 l
Ratio of time periods: T_2 / T_1 = √(l_2 / l_1) = √(1.44 l / l) = 1.2

solved_numericals.question: A clock with a brass pendulum keeps correct time at 20°C. If the room temperature rises to 40°C, how much time does the clock lose or gain in a day? (Coefficient of linear expansion of brass α = 1.9 × 10&sup5; /°C)
solution_steps: Given: ΔT = 40°C - 20°C = 20°C, α = 1.9 × 10^-5 /°C, Total time in a day t = 24 × 3600 s = 86400 s
Formula for time lost in time t: Δt = (1/2) α (ΔT) t

assumptions_and_limitations: The amplitude of oscillation must be very small (θ < 4°) so that sin(θ) ≈ θ is valid, ensuring linear simple harmonic motion.
The string is assumed strictly massless and inextensible; in real life, string mass and elasticity alter the effective moment of inertia and time period.
Air resistance and frictional damping at the support are neglected in the ideal model.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on the mass of the bob.
common_misconceptions.correct: The time period is independent of the mass of the bob.
common_misconceptions.why: Mass appears in both the restoring force (mg sin θ) and the moment of inertia (ml²), and thus cancels out in the expression T = 2π√(l/g).

common_misconceptions.wrong: A pendulum clock will run faster at high altitudes.
common_misconceptions.correct: A pendulum clock loses time (runs slow) at high altitudes.
common_misconceptions.why: Acceleration due to gravity g decreases with height above the Earth, increasing the time period T, meaning each oscillation takes longer.

quick_revision: T is proportional to square root of length and inversely proportional to square root of g.
Mass and amplitude (for small angles) do not affect the time period.
A seconds pendulum has a length of ~0.993 m and a period of 2 s.
